query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting Mn with a reactive element such as Si or Al in CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys promotes the formation of a stable, coherent, slow‐growing protective oxide layer above 900 °C in oxidizing or corrosive atmospheres by invoking the reactive element effect at the oxide scale grain boundaries.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state
generation.intervention: Replace X = Mn (baseline) with X = Si or Al
generation.conditions: Exposure to oxidizing or corrosive atmospheres at temperatures above 900 °C
generation.structural_mediator: A thin, continuous oxide layer enriched in SiO2 or Al2O3 that forms on the alloy surface
generation.mechanism: The reactive element effect: Si or Al segregates to the oxide grain boundaries, reducing intergranular diffusion and thermal strain during oxide growth. This inhibition of defect formation mitigates crack initiation and spallation, thereby stabilizing the protective oxide scale.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with Si or Al are expected to develop a more stable and adherent oxide scale with lower growth rates and reduced cracking/spallation compared to the Mn-containing counterpart under identical high-temperature conditions.
generation.baseline: CrFeCoNiMn high-entropy alloy under the same high-temperature oxidative or corrosive conditions
generation.boundary: Findings apply to CrFeCoNiX alloys in a single- or multiphase solid-solution state at temperatures above 900 °C and within typical oxidizing or corrosive service atmospheres.
generation.uncertainty: The extent of oxide scale stabilization and improvement in adhesion in Si- or Al-containing alloys may vary with specific compositional and microstructural factors. Long-term performance under varying environmental factors remains to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize equivalent batches of CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys with X = Mn (baseline), and with X = Si or Al. Expose all samples to temperatures above 900 °C in a controlled oxidizing or corrosive atmosphere for a predetermined duration. Characterize the oxide layer morphology, growth kinetics, composition, and adhesion.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and growth rate (using cross-sectional SEM)
Oxide composition and segregation profiles (using EDS or XPS)
Crack density and spallation occurrence (using optical and electron microscopy)
Adhesion strength of the oxide scale (via mechanical testing such as scratch or pull-off tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloys containing Si or Al do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxide scale growth, cracking, and spallation (or improved adhesion) compared to the Mn-containing alloy under identical test conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Replacing Mn with a reactive element like Si or Al in CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys promotes the formation of a stable, coherent, slow‐growing oxide layer above 900 °C because these elements facilitate the reactive element effect at the oxide scale grain boundaries, lowering diffusion and thermal strain that typically cause cracking and spallation.
drafts.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state
drafts.intervention: Substitute X = Mn (baseline) with X = Si or Al
drafts.conditions: Exposure to oxidizing or corrosive atmospheres at temperatures above 900 °C
drafts.structural_mediator: A thin, continuous oxide layer enriched in SiO2 or Al2O3 that forms at the surface
drafts.mechanism: The reactive element effect: Si or Al segregates to the oxide grain boundaries, reducing intergranular diffusion and mitigating stress accumulation during oxide growth, which in turn stabilizes the oxide layer and prevents crack initiation and spallation.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Alloys with Si or Al will develop a stable, coherent, and slow-growing protective oxide scale that does not crack or spall under prolonged high-temperature oxidation, in contrast to the Mn-containing alloy that forms a less adherent and more rapidly growing, unstable oxide.
drafts.baseline: CrFeCoNiMn high-entropy alloy under identical exposure conditions
drafts.boundary: Applicable to CrFeCoNiX alloys in a single- or multiphase solid-solution state, with exposures above 900 °C in oxidizing or corrosive atmospheres.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize comparable batches of CrFeCoNiX alloys with X = Mn, Si, and Al in a solid-solution state. Subject all samples to high-temperature (above 900 °C) oxidation tests in a controlled oxidative atmosphere for a fixed duration. Use microscopy and compositional analysis to assess oxide scale morphology and adhesion.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and growth rate (via cross-sectional SEM)
Compositional analysis of the oxide scale (using EDS or XPS)
Crack and spallation density (via optical and electron microscopy)
Adhesion strength of the oxide scale (via scratch tests or mechanical pull-off testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloys containing Si or Al do not show a statistically significant reduction in oxide scale cracking and spallation (and/or improved adhesion/stability) compared to the Mn-containing alloy under identical test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.
